name: McLeodganj (Dharamshala)
tagline: Tibetan temples and the Dhauladhar wall above Dharamshala
meta_description: McLeodganj guide: Tsuglagkhang temple, monk debates, Triund hike, Norbulingka crafts, Tibetan food, Volvo fares from Delhi, costs and stays in upper Dharamshala.
summary: McLeodganj is upper Dharamshala at about 2,080 m, home of the Dalai Lama and the Tibetan community in exile since 1960. Spend two or three nights: the Tsuglagkhang temple, monk debates, the Triund hike and Norbulingka's workshops. Best March to June and late September to November; July and August are very wet.
intro: McLeodganj began as a British cantonment on a spur above the Kangra valley in the mid-19th century, named after Sir Donald McLeod, Lieutenant Governor of Punjab. The 1905 Kangra earthquake wrecked it, and the town dwindled until 1960, when the 14th Dalai Lama moved here with the Tibetan government in exile. Today the two narrow roads of the main square, Temple Road and Jogiwara Road, are lined with Tibetan bakeries, bookshops and monasteries, and maroon robes are everywhere.

Behind the town rises the Dhauladhar, a granite wall that climbs from about 2,000 m to more than 4,500 m in a few kilometres. It catches the monsoon head-on, which makes Dharamshala one of the wettest places in India in July and August, and it gives McLeodganj its view: snow on the ridge for much of the year, directly above your breakfast table. The day hike to Triund, at about 2,850 m, is the easiest way up.

We use McLeodganj as a base for the Kangra valley. Bir and Billing, for paragliding and Tibetan monasteries, are 2.5 hours east. The Norbulingka Institute's craft workshops and the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives are lower down in Dharamshala. Chamba is about six hours north-west over the hills. Stay at least two nights, because the town rewards slow mornings: prayer wheels at the temple, coffee at a Tibetan bakery, and the afternoon debate in the monastery courtyard.
facts: Tibetan temples, Triund hike, momos and thukpa, Dhauladhar views

highlights.title: Tsuglagkhang temple complex
highlights.text: The main temple of the Tibetan community, opposite the Dalai Lama's residence, with Namgyal Monastery and the Tibet Museum inside the complex. Walk the kora path around it in the morning with local pilgrims spinning prayer wheels.

highlights.title: Monk debate in the courtyard
highlights.text: Most afternoons, young monks of Namgyal Monastery practise philosophical debate in the courtyard, clapping hands to mark a point. Visitors may watch quietly from the edges. No flash photography.

highlights.title: Triund day hike
highlights.text: About 9 km each way from McLeodganj, or 6–7 km from Galu temple, climbing to a grassy ridge at about 2,850 m under the Dhauladhar. Allow 6–8 hours return and start early.

highlights.title: Norbulingka Institute
highlights.text: Workshops near Sidhpur where Tibetan thangka painters, woodcarvers, metalworkers and tailors train and work, set in Japanese-style gardens. About 14 km below McLeodganj.

highlights.title: St John in the Wilderness
highlights.text: A stone church of 1852 in deodar forest 1.5 km below town, with Belgian stained-glass windows and the grave of Lord Elgin, a Viceroy of India who died nearby in 1863.

highlights.title: Bhagsu and Dharamkot
highlights.text: Two villages within walking distance: Bhagsu with its temple and small waterfall, and Dharamkot higher up, where cafés, meditation courses and quieter guesthouses sit among old Gaddi houses.

field_notes.fact: McLeod Ganj takes its name from Sir Donald Friell McLeod, a Lieutenant Governor of Punjab in the British period. The 'ganj' ending, meaning a market or neighbourhood, is common across north India.
The Church of St John in the Wilderness, built in 1852, holds the memorial of James Bruce, the 8th Earl of Elgin, Viceroy of India, who died at Dharamshala in 1863 and was buried in the churchyard.
field_notes.source: St. John in the Wilderness Church

field_notes.fact: The 1905 Kangra earthquake, of roughly magnitude 7.8, killed around 20,000 people across the region and destroyed most of the buildings in the Dharamshala cantonment and McLeod Ganj.

local_word.meaning: a greeting meaning roughly 'blessings and good luck', used for hello and on Losar

costs: Plate of momos at a Tibetan café

how_to_reach.text: Kangra airport at Gaggal is about 20 km and 45–60 minutes from McLeodganj by taxi, with daily flights from Delhi in good weather. Taxis from the airport cost around ₹1,000–1,500.

HRTC Volvos from Delhi's Kashmere Gate run overnight to Dharamshala and many continue to McLeodganj, about 10–12 hours. Private Volvos leave Majnu ka Tilla, Delhi's Tibetan colony, for McLeodganj every evening. Local buses link Dharamshala and McLeodganj through the day.

The nearest broad-gauge stations are Pathankot (about 90 km, 3 hours) and Una (about 120 km). The narrow-gauge Kangra Valley Railway from Pathankot stops at Kangra Mandir, but it is slow and services are sometimes suspended.
From Delhi via Chandigarh, Una and Kangra, about 480 km and 10–12 hours. The road from Dharamshala up to McLeodganj is steep and congested; the Dharamshala Skyway ropeway is an alternative.

where_to_stay: Saver: McLeodganj, Bhagsu and Dharamkot have hostels and family guesthouses from ₹500 for a dorm bed and ₹1,200–2,000 for a simple double; Dharamkot is the quietest. Comfort: mid-range hotels line Jogiwara Road and the Dharamshala road, and Chonor House, built and run by the Norbulingka Institute, has Tibetan-themed rooms a few steps from the main temple. Signature: the best large hotels are lower down in the Dharamshala area and the Kangra valley; we pair them with a McLeodganj day, or use Chonor House for its location and character.
tips: Walk the kora around Tsuglagkhang clockwise, as pilgrims do, and do not point your feet at altars inside.
Check the Dalai Lama's public teaching schedule on his official website; the town fills when he teaches.
Leave for Triund by 7 am so you are back down before afternoon clouds and rain.
Carry a rain shell any month; showers build over the Dhauladhar even in spring.
Buy Tibetan crafts at Norbulingka or cooperative shops, where the money reaches the artisans.

experiences.title: Tsuglagkhang temple and the monk debate
experiences.best_time: Morning kora 7 am; debate around 2–4 pm
experiences.summary: Walk the morning kora around the Dalai Lama's temple with Tibetan pilgrims, visit the main prayer hall and the Tibet Museum, then return in the afternoon to watch Namgyal monks practise debate in the courtyard.
body: The Tsuglagkhang complex, a short walk down Temple Road from the main square, is the spiritual centre of the Tibetan community in exile. It holds the main temple, the Dalai Lama's private monastery of Namgyal and the Tibet Museum, and faces his residence. Start with the kora, the clockwise walking circuit around the complex on a forest path lined with prayer wheels, prayer flags and carved mani stones. Older Tibetans walk it every morning with prayer beads in hand.

Inside, the main hall holds a large gilded Shakyamuni Buddha, with images of Avalokiteshvara and Padmasambhava nearby. Security staff check bags at the gate, and cameras may be restricted in the prayer halls. Remove shoes where asked, walk clockwise, and keep your voice low. The Tibet Museum on the ground floor tells the story of Tibet and of the exile community in photographs and documents; plan 45 minutes.

In the afternoon, monks of Namgyal Monastery often hold debate practice in the courtyard. One monk sits while another stands, poses a question on Buddhist philosophy and claps his hands loudly to drive the point home. It is study, not performance, so watch from the side, stay quiet and avoid flash. Debate does not happen every day; ask at the gate in the morning.

faqs.q: Can I meet the Dalai Lama in McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Private audiences are rare and arranged through his office. Public teachings are held at the Tsuglagkhang several times a year, and anyone can attend after registering with the security office with a passport or ID and photos. The schedule is on his official website.

faqs.q: Is photography allowed inside the Tsuglagkhang?
faqs.a: Rules vary: phones and cameras are often allowed in the courtyard but restricted inside prayer halls, and always forbidden during teachings. Never photograph monks or worshippers at prayer without permission. Follow the signs and guards on the day.

faqs.q: When do the monks debate in McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Usually in the afternoon on many weekdays during the monastic term, in the courtyard of the Tsuglagkhang complex. There is no fixed public timetable, and holidays or teachings change it. Ask at the gate or your guesthouse in the morning.

experiences.title: Day hike to Triund ridge
experiences.cost: Free; guide ₹1,500–2,500; forest fee may apply
experiences.summary: Climb about 900 m from Galu temple above Dharamkot to the open ridge of Triund at roughly 2,850 m, with the Dhauladhar wall in front and the Kangra valley behind. Steady, well-trodden and the classic hike from McLeodganj.
body: Most hikers walk or take a taxi to Galu Devi temple above Dharamkot, where the trail begins. From there it is about 6–7 km to Triund on a stone path that zigzags through oak and rhododendron forest, with tea shops at intervals. The last section, sometimes called the 22 bends, is the steepest. Fit walkers reach the top in 3–4 hours; take more time if you are coming straight from the plains.

Triund is a grassy ridge at about 2,850 m. On one side the Dhauladhar rises sharply to the snow-streaked rock of the main ridge; on the other the Kangra valley falls away to the plains. In spring the forest is red with rhododendron. Some walkers continue another hour or two to the Snowline café area near Laka Got for closer views, but that adds time and should only be done in clear weather.

Overnight camping at Triund has been restricted at times by the forest department and the administration. Rules change, so check current status before you travel. Leave nothing behind: carry all plastic down. Weather turns quickly here, and the ridge is exposed to lightning in thunderstorms, so turn back if clouds build fast. In winter the upper trail can be icy; go with a local guide.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Triund trek?
faqs.a: Moderate. It is about 6–7 km one way from Galu temple with roughly 900 m of climbing, on a clear stone path. Fit beginners manage it in a day. The final bends are steep. Good shoes, water, a rain jacket and snacks are essential.

faqs.q: Can I camp overnight at Triund?
faqs.a: At times overnight camping has been allowed through registered operators, and at other times it has been banned by the authorities. The rules change from season to season. Check current status before you travel, and never camp on the ridge in thunderstorms.

faqs.q: Is Triund safe for solo women?
faqs.a: Yes in daylight; the trail is busy with hikers and tea-shop owners. Start early, tell your guesthouse your plan, and avoid descending after dark. In poor weather or winter, hire a registered local guide. Keep your phone charged; signal is patchy.

experiences.title: Tibetan crafts at Norbulingka
experiences.summary: Visit the Norbulingka Institute near Sidhpur, where Tibetan artists train in thangka painting, woodcarving, statue-making and tailoring, then stop at the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives in lower Dharamshala on the way back.
body: Norbulingka was set up in the late 1980s to keep traditional Tibetan arts alive in exile, and it takes its name from the Dalai Lama's old summer palace in Lhasa. The campus near Sidhpur, about 14 km below McLeodganj, is laid out with small bridges, streams and Japanese-style gardens. Walk through the workshops and you can watch thangka painters grind mineral pigments, woodcarvers cut altar panels and metalworkers beat copper into statues.

The temple on site has a large gilded Buddha and wall paintings of the lineage of the Dalai Lamas. There is also a doll museum showing Tibetan regional dress. The shop sells work made on site, at fixed prices, and the café is good for lunch. Chonor House, the hotel in McLeodganj, was built and is run by the same institute.

On the way back, stop at the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, founded by the 14th Dalai Lama in 1970, which holds manuscripts, thangkas and a small museum. It also runs courses in Tibetan language and Buddhist philosophy that visitors can join. Both places keep weekday hours and close on some holidays, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Norbulingka from McLeodganj?
faqs.a: About 14 km, or 40–50 minutes by taxi via Dharamshala. Local buses run to Sidhpur but involve a change. Many visitors combine it with the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives and Gyuto monastery on a half-day taxi loop.

faqs.q: Can I buy thangkas at Norbulingka?
faqs.a: Yes. The institute's shop sells thangkas, carvings, statues and textiles made on site, at fixed prices. Large thangkas take months to paint and are priced accordingly. Ask for a certificate or receipt for export or gifting.

faqs.q: Can visitors study at the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives?
faqs.a: Yes. The library runs regular courses in Buddhist philosophy and Tibetan language, open to visitors who register at the office. Classes are typically held on weekdays. Check the current schedule and fees on arrival or on the library's official website.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Dharamshala and McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Dharamshala is the larger town and district headquarters, lower down at about 1,400 m. McLeodganj is the upper part at about 2,080 m, where the Dalai Lama lives and most travellers stay. They are about 9 km apart by road, linked by buses, taxis and a ropeway.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Two to three nights. One day for the Tsuglagkhang, kora, Bhagsu and Dharamkot, one for the Triund hike, and half a day for Norbulingka and the Tibetan library. Add a night if you want to attend a meditation or language course.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit McLeodganj?
faqs.a: March to June and late September to November. Spring has rhododendrons and good hiking; autumn has the clearest views of the Dhauladhar. July and August bring very heavy rain. Winter is cold but bright, with snow on the ridge.

faqs.q: How much does a McLeodganj trip cost?
faqs.a: On a saver budget, about ₹1,800–2,800 a day for a hostel or guesthouse, Tibetan café meals and local buses, plus ₹2,400–3,400 for a return Volvo from Delhi. A comfort stay with a good hotel and taxis costs ₹6,000–10,000 a day per person.

faqs.q: Is McLeodganj safe for solo women?
faqs.a: Yes. It is one of the most popular hill towns for solo women in India, with hostels, courses and cafés full of other travellers. Use normal care at night on unlit lanes to Dharamkot and Bhagsu, and do not hike alone in bad weather.

faqs.q: What food should I try in McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Tibetan momos, thukpa noodle soup, thenthuk hand-pulled noodles, tingmo steamed bread and butter tea. Bakeries sell cinnamon rolls and brown bread. For Himachali food, look for siddu and Kangri dham in Dharamshala's lower bazaar.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and good network in McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Yes. There are several ATMs around the main square and Jogiwara Road, and all major networks have good 4G. Higher villages like Dharamkot have weaker signal in places. Most cafés accept UPI; keep cash for taxis and small stalls.

faqs.q: Can I see snow in McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Snow falls on the Dhauladhar ridge above town most winters and is visible from McLeodganj from about November to April. Snow in the town itself is occasional, usually in January or February. For snow underfoot, hike towards Triund in winter with a guide.

Yes, with planning. The town is compact but steep, with narrow lanes and few pavements. Choose a hotel near the main square or Temple Road with vehicle access, use taxis for longer distances and skip Triund. The temple complex is on one level.
